title: Apathies and Artifices in Education (Part 1 of 3)
author: AI Edu Simplified
summary: This is the first of three posts examining structural crises of higher education that AI has surfaced rather than created. Part 1 focuses on 'militant apathy' -- students who returned from pandemic-era remote learning with pervasive disengagement. The author's central argument is that the apathy was not primarily caused by the pandemic but by a contradiction higher education never honestly addressed: students were told online learning was still their full college education (worth full tuition), then summoned back to campus on the premise that in-person learning is significantly better -- a logical contradiction students felt as falseness. AI has deepened the same fault line: students see assignments that AI can complete instantly and ask, implicitly, 'really?' -- not because they think the work doesn't matter, but because they've been given only grades as a reason to do it, and grades already felt like hoop-jumping before AI made the stakes explicit. Higher education's course structures were never designed because they were pedagogically optimal; they were designed because they were manageable and scalable -- and AI has made that efficiency-over-pedagogy logic impossible to ignore. The piece distinguishes itself from the view that AI created students' apathy; instead, AI has made pre-existing structural contradictions visible and urgent.
points: Student 'militant apathy' post-pandemic was a rational response to an institutional contradiction: students were told online learning was real college, then told they had to return because in-person is better, without anyone owning the contradiction -- a falseness students felt without always being able to name.

AI has extended the same logic: students see AI completing assignments instantly and ask 'really?' -- not because work doesn't matter, but because grades-as-sole-motivation already felt like compliance rather than genuine learning before AI made the question inescapable.

Higher education's course structures (semesters, credit hours, seat time, text-heavy assignments) were designed for manageability and scale, not because they are the best way people learn -- AI has exposed that efficiency-over-pedagogy foundation.

The 'ruling contradiction' is that education claims to be about community and care while being structured around institutional efficiency -- AI and the pandemic both strip away the scaffolding that obscured this gap.
The remedy is not abandoning rigor but providing a better reason: structures that make students feel that assignments build something in them rather than requiring them to prove they did the thing.
quotes: When we summoned them back, we did not really account for what had just happened. We didn't own the contradiction. We said, 'No, no, you have to come back to the classroom. Learning is better face-to-face.' There is a falseness there that higher education hasn't owned up to.

AI has extended that same dynamic. Now the apathy is not just about the classroom; it is about what we ask students to do. Students are looking at us, looking at these tools, looking at the world they are being told they are preparing for, and asking: really?

I do not think the answer is that the work does not matter. Reading matters. Writing matters. Research matters. Thinking carefully and making meaning across complexity absolutely matters. But we need a better reason than a grade.

We have to reconcile that higher education is structured around efficiency. Not because faculty do not care, but because we inherited systems built around convenience, grading, semesters, credit hours, seat time, and text-heavy assignments that were never necessarily designed because they were the best way people learn.
The ruling contradiction is that education is structured around efficiency and convenience to the institution's benefit -- and moments like the pandemic and now AI make that glaringly evident.
